# What this vignette covers

A kernel-weighted mean tells you the average value of a continuous raster
around a survey point. Two points can share the same average elevation or
canopy height while one sits in smooth terrain and the other in rugged terrain.
Surface texture metrics describe that difference. `surface_var()` computes six
of them from a continuous raster within a neighborhood of each survey point,
and each metric then enters your model as a covariate.

This vignette shows what each family of metrics measures, which scales you can
fix and which you can estimate, and how to read a fitted coefficient in the
metric's own units. You will add a roughness metric to the count model from
`vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")`, then estimate the scale of
roughness from counts simulated with a known answer. Read the Quick Start
first. `vignette("v04-landscape-metrics", package = "multiScaleR")`
follows the same steps for categorical rasters.

# Know what each metric family measures

Every metric summarizes the cells in a neighborhood of a survey point. By
default the neighborhood is a circle with a hard edge, so each cell inside it
counts equally. The table gives the ecological meaning and the units of each
family.

| Family | Metrics | What it measures | Units |
|:-------|:--------|:-----------------|:------|
| Dispersion | `sa` (average roughness), `sq` (root mean square roughness) | How much the surface varies around its local mean, such as rugged against level terrain or a patchy against an even canopy | Units of the raster |
| Distribution shape | `ssk` (skewness), `sku` (excess kurtosis) | Whether a few unusually high or low values stand out from the rest of the neighborhood | Unitless |
| Local geometry | `sdq` (root mean square slope), `sdr` (surface area ratio) | How steeply the surface changes from one cell to the next, and how much surface area that relief adds | `sdq` as rise over run, in raster units per map unit. `sdr` as a percentage |

Four details apply across the table.

- **`sa` and `sq` measure the same idea.** `sa` is the mean absolute deviation
  from the neighborhood mean. `sq` is the standard deviation, which squares the
  deviations and so responds more to a few extreme cells.
- **Shape is read against a normal distribution.** `ssk` is positive when
  occasional high values dominate and negative when occasional low values do.
  `sku` is 0 for a normal distribution of values. Both return `NA` for a flat
  neighborhood.
- **Geometry needs matching units.** `sdq` divides the change in value by the
  cell size, and `sdr` is the percentage by which the three-dimensional surface
  area exceeds the flat area. Read them as a slope and an area ratio only when
  the raster values and the map share units, as elevation in meters does.
- **Agreement with `geodiv`.** `sa`, `sq`, `ssk`, and `sku` match the `geodiv`
  package. `geodiv::sdq()` assumes a cell size of one, so it equals `sdq` here
  multiplied by the cell size. `geodiv::sdr()` rescales the surface to a unit
  range before it computes area, so its values differ from `sdr` here.

The help page `?msr_vars` defines every metric.

# Decide which scales to fix and which to estimate

The scale of a covariate is the distance over which the surface is summarized.
The `radius` and `weighted` arguments decide whether you fix that distance or
estimate it.

| How you write the covariate | Metrics | What sets the scale | What `multiScale_optim()` reports |
|:----------------------------|:--------|:--------------------|:----------------------------------|
| `surface_var("elev", metric = "sq", radius = 500)` | All six | You do. The metric is computed once within 500 map units | No scale. The metric is an ordinary covariate |
| `surface_var("elev", metric = "sq")` | All six | The data. The hard radius is estimated with the model | The radius, without a standard error. Profile-likelihood limits come from `summary(fit, profile = TRUE)` |
| `surface_var("elev", metric = "sq", weighted = TRUE)` | `sa`, `sq`, `ssk`, `sku` | The data. Cells are weighted by the model's kernel, and its width, sigma, is estimated | Sigma with a standard error and confidence interval |
| `kernel_var("elev")` | The mean, not a texture metric | The data. Sigma is estimated with the model | Sigma with a standard error and confidence interval |

With `weighted = TRUE` the scale is always estimated, so supplying `radius` as
well is an error. The geometry metrics `sdq` and `sdr` have no weighted form.

> **What this means for your study.** Fix the radius when you have a biological
> reason for a distance. When the scale of heterogeneity is itself the
> question, use `weighted = TRUE`. Kernel weights change smoothly with sigma,
> so you get a standard error, and the estimate reads as a scale of effect in
> the same way a kernel mean does.

# Work through an example

## Load the data

The example uses the counts, survey points, and raster from the Quick Start.
The counts were simulated to respond to the kernel-weighted mean of `land1`
(sigma of 250 m, effect of -0.5) and of `land2` (sigma of 500 m, effect of
0.7). No texture metric entered the simulation.

```{r load-data}
data("landscape_counts")   # data frame: counts and one site-level covariate
dat <- landscape_counts

data("surv_pts")           # survey locations (an sf object from the package)
pts <- vect(surv_pts)      # convert to a terra SpatVector

# Three landscape layers on one grid, in meters
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))
```

`land3` is a continuous layer with values from 0 to 1 and broad, smooth
patches. Think of it as elevation or canopy height. It supplies the texture
metrics in this vignette.

```{r plot-inputs, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "***The continuous land3 layer, alone and with the survey points.***"}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(land_rast$land3, main = "land3")
plot(land_rast$land3, main = "Survey points")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## Define the covariates

`msr_vars()` names each model covariate and says how to derive it from a
source layer. The model below keeps the two kernel means from the Quick Start
and adds the roughness of `land3` within 500 m.

```{r define-vars}
scale_vars <- msr_vars(
  land1_prop   = kernel_var("land1"),     # proportion of habitat, sigma estimated
  land2_mean   = kernel_var("land2"),     # mean of land2, sigma estimated
  land3_sq_500 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq",
                             radius = 500)   # roughness of land3 within 500 m
)

scale_vars[, c("covariate", "source", "type", "metric", "radius", "optimize")]
```

**How to read the output:** Each row is one model covariate. `source` is the
raster layer it comes from. `optimize` is `TRUE` for the two kernel covariates,
whose sigma will be estimated, and `FALSE` for the roughness metric, whose
radius is fixed at 500 m.

## Compute the metrics at the survey points

Pass the specification to `kernel_prep()` through `scale_vars`. It extracts the
cells within `max_D` of each point and computes every covariate.

```{r kernel-prep}
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,          # survey locations
  raster_stack = land_rast,    # source layers named in scale_vars
  max_D        = 1700,         # largest distance (m) considered
  kernel       = "gaussian",   # kernel for the two kernel covariates
  scale_vars   = scale_vars,
  verbose      = FALSE
)

# Mean and standard deviation of each covariate, in its own units
round(sapply(kernel_inputs$scl_params, function(x) x), 3)
```

**How to read the output:** `kernel_inputs$kernel_dat` holds the covariates
after centering and scaling, which is what the model uses. `scl_params` keeps
the mean and standard deviation that were removed, in the units of each
metric. Roughness of `land3` within 500 m averages
`r round(kernel_inputs$scl_params$mean["land3_sq_500"], 3)` across the survey
points, with a standard deviation of
`r round(kernel_inputs$scl_params$sd["land3_sq_500"], 3)`. `sq` is in the units
of the raster, and `land3` runs from 0 to 1, so a typical buffer holds values
that sit about a tenth of that range from their local mean. The rows for the
two kernel covariates are provisional, because they were computed at a
starting sigma.

## Fit the model

Fit the starting model with the derived covariates, then let
`multiScale_optim()` estimate the two kernel scales. The roughness metric was
computed once and stays as it is.

```{r fit-model}
df <- data.frame(dat, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)

# Starting model: formula and family carry through to the optimizer
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1_prop + land2_mean + land3_sq_500,
           family = poisson(),
           data   = df)

# Estimate sigma for land1_prop and land2_mean
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = mod,
                        kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        verbose       = FALSE)
```

## Read the estimated scale

```{r summary}
summary(opt)
```

```{r read-scale, include = FALSE}
est    <- summary(opt)$opt_scale     # sigma, SE, and 95% interval (m)
dist90 <- kernel_dist(opt)           # radius holding 90% of kernel weight (m)
```

**How to read the `summary()` output:** The scale tables list only the two
kernel covariates. Sigma for `land1_prop` is `r round(est["land1_prop", "Mean"])`
m, with a 95% interval of `r round(est["land1_prop", "2.5%"])` to
`r round(est["land1_prop", "97.5%"])` m that contains the true 250 m. Sigma for
`land2_mean` is `r round(est["land2_mean", "Mean"])` m, against a true 500 m.
The distance table converts each sigma to the radius that holds 90% of the
kernel weight, which is `r round(dist90["land1_prop", "Mean"])` m for
`land1_prop` and `r round(dist90["land2_mean", "Mean"])` m for `land2_mean`.
Roughness is absent from the scale tables because you set its radius. It
appears only in the regression table, as an ordinary covariate measured within
500 m.

## Interpret a coefficient in the metric's units

The regression coefficients are on the log scale, because the model is Poisson
with a log link. Each one describes a change of one standard deviation,
because the covariates were standardized. Two steps turn a coefficient into a
statement about the metric. Divide by the metric's standard deviation to get
the effect of one unit, then exponentiate to get a multiplicative change in
the expected count.

```{r coef-units}
beta <- coef(opt$opt_mod)              # log scale, per one standard deviation
ci   <- confint.default(opt$opt_mod)   # Wald 95% limits, log scale
sds  <- opt$scl_params$sd              # one standard deviation, in metric units

# A step that is easy to picture, in the units of the metric
step <- c(land3_sq_500 = 0.01)         # 0.01 more roughness, in land3 units
m <- names(step)

effect <- data.frame(
  Covariate  = m,
  SD         = sds[m],
  Step       = step,
  Multiplier = exp(beta[m]  * step / sds[m]),   # change in expected count
  Lower      = exp(ci[m, 1] * step / sds[m]),
  Upper      = exp(ci[m, 2] * step / sds[m])
)
knitr::kable(effect, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

**How to read the table:** `Multiplier` is the factor by which the expected
count changes when the metric rises by `Step`, with the other covariates held
constant. An increase of 0.01 in the roughness of `land3` within 500 m
multiplies the expected count by `r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Multiplier[1])`,
with a 95% interval of `r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Lower[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Upper[1])`. The interval includes 1, which means no
change. That is the right answer here, because roughness was not used to
simulate the counts. The interval treats the estimated sigma values as known,
as explained in `vignette("v09-estimates-and-intervals", package = "multiScaleR")`.

# Estimate the scale of a metric

The running example has no roughness effect to recover, so this section
simulates one. The counts below respond to the kernel-weighted roughness of
`land3`, with a Gaussian kernel whose sigma is 300 m and an effect of 0.5 on
the log scale for each standard deviation of roughness.

```{r sim-truth}
# Kernel-weighted roughness: cells are weighted by the model's kernel
weighted_vars <- msr_vars(
  land3_sq = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", weighted = TRUE)
)

# Roughness at a sigma of 300 m, the scale used to simulate the counts
truth_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  max_D        = 1500,
  kernel       = "gaussian",
  scale_vars   = weighted_vars,
  sigma        = 300,              # compute the covariate at this sigma
  verbose      = FALSE
)

set.seed(1)
# kernel_dat is standardized, so 0.5 is the effect of one standard deviation
sim_counts <- rpois(100, exp(0.5 + 0.5 * truth_inputs$kernel_dat$land3_sq))
```

To estimate the scale, prepare the same specification without a sigma.
Everything else is the usual workflow.

```{r sim-fit}
free_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  max_D        = 1500,             # sigma is searched within this distance
  kernel       = "gaussian",
  scale_vars   = weighted_vars,
  verbose      = FALSE
)

sim_df  <- data.frame(counts = sim_counts, free_inputs$kernel_dat)
sim_mod <- glm(counts ~ land3_sq, family = poisson(), data = sim_df)

sim_opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = sim_mod,
                            kernel_inputs = free_inputs,
                            verbose       = FALSE)

# Sigma with its standard error and 95% interval, in meters
sim_scale <- summary(sim_opt)$opt_scale
round(sim_scale, 1)

# Radius that holds 90% of the kernel weight, in meters
sim_dist <- kernel_dist(sim_opt)
round(sim_dist)
```

**How to read the output:** `Mean` in the first table is the estimated sigma,
`r round(sim_scale["land3_sq", "Mean"])` m, with a 95% interval of
`r round(sim_scale["land3_sq", "2.5%"])` to
`r round(sim_scale["land3_sq", "97.5%"])` m that contains the 300 m used to
simulate the counts. Unlike a hard radius, a kernel-weighted metric has a
standard error. Sigma is a kernel width, not a radius. The second table
converts it to an effective distance. The variability of `land3` within about
`r round(sim_dist["land3_sq", "Mean"])` m of a survey point shapes the count.

```{r sim-profile, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***AICc across candidate sigma values for kernel-weighted roughness. The dashed line marks the estimate.***"}
# Refit the model at 15 candidate sigma values
plot(profile_sigma(sim_opt, n_pts = 15, verbose = FALSE))
```

**How to read this plot:** Lower AICc means better support. A single deep
trough near the dashed line means the data identify the scale. A flat profile,
or one that keeps falling toward the edge of the search range, would mean the
data say little about it.

Interpret the coefficient as before. The standard deviation now belongs to
roughness at the estimated sigma.

```{r sim-coef}
sim_beta <- coef(sim_opt$opt_mod)["land3_sq"]             # per standard deviation
sim_ci   <- confint.default(sim_opt$opt_mod)["land3_sq", ]
sim_sd   <- sim_opt$scl_params$sd["land3_sq"]             # land3 units, fitted sigma

# Change in expected count for 0.01 more roughness
sim_effect <- exp(c(Estimate = unname(sim_beta), Lower = sim_ci[[1]],
                    Upper = sim_ci[[2]]) * 0.01 / sim_sd)
round(sim_effect, 3)

# The value used in the simulation, on the same footing
round(exp(0.5 * 0.01 / truth_inputs$scl_params$sd["land3_sq"]), 3)
```

**How to read the output:** At the estimated scale, each additional 0.01 of
roughness multiplies the expected count by
`r sprintf("%.2f", sim_effect["Estimate"])`, an increase of
`r round(100 * (sim_effect["Estimate"] - 1))`%. The 95% interval runs from
`r sprintf("%.2f", sim_effect["Lower"])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", sim_effect["Upper"])` and contains the simulated value on
the last line.

```{r sim-marginal, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***Expected count across the observed range of kernel-weighted roughness at the estimated sigma.***"}
plot_marginal_effects(sim_opt)
```

**How to read this plot:** The horizontal axis is roughness in the units of
`land3`, not the standardized covariate, so you can read expected counts
directly against the metric. The shaded band is a 95% confidence band for the
expected count that treats the estimated sigma as known.

> **What this means for your study.** Changing the scale of a texture metric
> changes the quantity, not only its smoothness. A small neighborhood measures
> fine-grained texture. A large one also takes in broad gradients and
> patchiness. The estimated scale is the neighborhood size at which
> variability best explains the response.

To estimate a hard radius in place of a kernel sigma, write
`surface_var("land3", metric = "sq")` with neither `radius` nor `weighted`.
All six metrics accept that form. `summary()` then reports the radius without
a standard error, as it does for a landscape metric, and
`vignette("v04-landscape-metrics", package = "multiScaleR")` shows how to
read that output.

# Map the metrics

## Map the covariates of a fitted model

`kernel_scale.raster()` applies each covariate definition to the whole raster.
Given a fitted model, it uses the estimated sigma for kernel covariates and
the stated radius for fixed-radius metrics.

```{r project, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "***The covariates of the fitted model, in their own units.***"}
projected <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land_rast,
                                 multiScaleR  = opt,       # the fitted object
                                 verbose      = FALSE)
names(projected)

plot(projected[[1:3]], nc = 3, mar = c(2, 2, 2, 5))   # room for each legend
```

**How to read these plots:** Each layer carries the name of a model covariate
and is in that covariate's units. `land1_prop` and `land2_mean` are smoothed
averages. `land3_sq_500` is different in kind. It is high where `land3` changes
within 500 m and low where `land3` is locally uniform, so it marks transitions
between patches and not the patches themselves. The fourth layer, `site`, is a
constant zero. `site` was measured at the survey points and has no raster, so
the function adds a placeholder to let the stack go straight to
`terra::predict()`.

To predict from the model, add `scale_center = TRUE` so the layers are
standardized as the model's covariates were, and `clamp = TRUE` to stay inside
the fitted range. `vignette("v03-map-predictions", package = "multiScaleR")`
covers prediction maps.

## Map a metric without a model

You do not need a fitted model to map a metric. Pass a specification in which
every covariate has a fixed radius.

```{r standalone-multiscale, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "***Root mean square roughness of land3 at three radii.***"}
sq_multi <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(
    sq_200 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 200),
    sq_500 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 500),
    sq_900 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 900)
  ),
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Mean of each surface, in land3 units
round(t(global(sq_multi, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)), 3)

plot(sq_multi, nc = 3, mar = c(2, 2, 2, 5))   # room for each legend
```

**How to read these plots:** The same metric looks different at each radius. At
200 m the surface picks out local texture, so roughness is patchy. At 900 m
each buffer spans more of the broad gradient in `land3`, so the surface is
smoother and its mean is higher. This is the reason an estimated scale
matters.

## Compare the six metrics

Map all six metrics at one radius, then check how they relate at the survey
points before you put more than one in a model.

```{r six-metrics, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.4, fig.cap = "***The six texture metrics of land3 within 500 m.***"}
six <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(
    sa  = surface_var("land3", metric = "sa",  radius = 500),
    sq  = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq",  radius = 500),
    ssk = surface_var("land3", metric = "ssk", radius = 500),
    sku = surface_var("land3", metric = "sku", radius = 500),
    sdq = surface_var("land3", metric = "sdq", radius = 500),
    sdr = surface_var("land3", metric = "sdr", radius = 500)
  ),
  verbose = FALSE
)

plot(six, nc = 3, mar = c(2, 2, 2, 5))   # room for each legend

# Correlation among the metrics at the survey points
round(cor(extract(six, pts, ID = FALSE)), 2)
```

**How to read the output:** `sa` and `sq` share one pattern, and so do `sdq`
and `sdr`. Their correlations at the survey points round to 1, so a model can
use only one member of each pair. `ssk` and `sku` show different patterns
because they describe the shape of the distribution of values and not its
spread. The values of `sdq` and `sdr` are tiny here because `land3` is a
unitless layer on a grid with 20 m cells.

## Compare a hard radius with kernel weights

Mapping a kernel-weighted metric needs the kernel and its sigma, because no
fitted model supplies them.

```{r weighted-vs-hard, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "***Roughness of land3 within a 500 m hard radius, and with Gaussian weights at a sigma of 500 m.***"}
sq_hard <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(sq_hard = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq",
                                                radius = 500)),
  verbose      = FALSE
)

sq_weighted <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(sq_weighted = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq",
                                                    weighted = TRUE)),
  sigma        = 500,          # kernel width for the weighted metric (m)
  kernel       = "gaussian",
  verbose      = FALSE
)

plot(c(sq_hard, sq_weighted))
```

**How to read these plots:** Both maps show the local roughness of `land3`.
The weighted map is smoother for two reasons. Nearby cells count more than
distant ones, and a Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 500 m places 90% of its
weight within about 1,075 m, a wider area than the 500 m circle.

# Check these before you fit

- **Raster type.** `surface_var()` expects continuous values. For class codes
  use `vignette("v04-landscape-metrics", package = "multiScaleR")`.
- **Correlated metrics.** Texture metrics from one layer often move together.
  Check their correlations, as above, and keep one member of a correlated
  pair.
- **Variation among points.** A metric that barely varies among survey points
  cannot explain the response. Check `kernel_inputs$scl_params$sd` before
  fitting.
- **Enough cells.** Shape metrics are noisier than dispersion metrics and need
  many cells in the neighborhood to be stable.
- **Method support.** The table below lists what each form of a texture metric
  accepts. `vignette("v07-fitting-methods", package = "multiScaleR")` gives
  the full matrix.

| Form | Metrics | Fitting methods |
|:-----|:--------|:----------------|
| Fixed radius | All six | Every backend of `multiScale_optim()` and `multiScale_bayes()`, because the metric is an ordinary numeric covariate |
| Estimated hard radius | All six | `multiScale_optim()` with the default `backend = "refit"` |
| Kernel weighted | `sa`, `ssk`, `sku` | `multiScale_optim()` with the default `backend = "refit"` |
| Kernel weighted | `sq` | The default backend, and with a Gaussian or exponential kernel the `profile_glm`, `joint_nb2`, `conditional_logit`, and `joint_mixed` backends and `multiScale_bayes()` |

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

# 1. Load the data
data("landscape_counts"); data("surv_pts")
dat       <- landscape_counts
pts       <- vect(surv_pts)
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))

# 2. Define the covariates: two kernel means and one fixed-radius metric
scale_vars <- msr_vars(
  land1_prop   = kernel_var("land1"),
  land2_mean   = kernel_var("land2"),
  land3_sq_500 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 500)
)

# 3. Compute the covariates at the survey points
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                             max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
                             scale_vars = scale_vars, verbose = FALSE)
kernel_inputs$scl_params            # mean and SD of each metric, in its units

# 4. Fit the model and estimate the kernel scales
df  <- data.frame(dat, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1_prop + land2_mean + land3_sq_500,
           family = poisson(), data = df)
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod, kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        verbose = FALSE)
summary(opt)                        # sigma, effective distance, regression table

# 5. Read a metric coefficient in the metric's units
beta <- coef(opt$opt_mod)
sds  <- opt$scl_params$sd
exp(beta["land3_sq_500"] * 0.01 / sds["land3_sq_500"])   # per 0.01 of roughness

# 6. Estimate the scale of a metric: weight it with the kernel
weighted_vars <- msr_vars(
  land3_sq = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", weighted = TRUE)
)
truth_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
                            max_D = 1500, kernel = "gaussian",
                            scale_vars = weighted_vars, sigma = 300,
                            verbose = FALSE)
set.seed(1)
sim_counts  <- rpois(100, exp(0.5 + 0.5 * truth_inputs$kernel_dat$land3_sq))
free_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
                           max_D = 1500, kernel = "gaussian",
                           scale_vars = weighted_vars, verbose = FALSE)
sim_df  <- data.frame(counts = sim_counts, free_inputs$kernel_dat)
sim_mod <- glm(counts ~ land3_sq, family = poisson(), data = sim_df)
sim_opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = sim_mod, kernel_inputs = free_inputs,
                            verbose = FALSE)
summary(sim_opt)$opt_scale                     # sigma, SE, and 95% interval
kernel_dist(sim_opt)                           # radius holding 90% of the weight
plot(profile_sigma(sim_opt, n_pts = 15, verbose = FALSE))   # AICc by sigma
plot_marginal_effects(sim_opt)                 # expected count against roughness

# 7. Map the covariates of a fitted model, or a metric on its own
projected <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land_rast,
                                 multiScaleR = opt, verbose = FALSE)
sq_multi  <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(
    sq_200 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 200),
    sq_500 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 500),
    sq_900 = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq", radius = 900)),
  verbose = FALSE)
sq_weighted <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast["land3"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(sq_weighted = surface_var("land3", metric = "sq",
                                                    weighted = TRUE)),
  sigma = 500, kernel = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE)
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `msr_vars()` | Collect named covariate definitions into one specification |
| `kernel_var()` | Define a kernel-weighted mean whose sigma is estimated |
| `surface_var()` | Define a texture metric from a continuous raster, with a fixed radius, an estimated radius, or kernel weights |
| `kernel_prep()` | Compute the covariates at the survey points and store their means and standard deviations |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate every free sigma and radius together with the regression coefficients |
| `summary()`, `kernel_dist()` | Report scales, effective distances, and the regression table |
| `profile_sigma()` | Show how well the data identify each scale |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Draw the expected response against each covariate in its own units |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Map covariates, with or without a fitted model |
